title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
author: lasu
summary: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks. title: Google Trends for 100 keywords without failed runs: a pipeline for SEO and e-commerce teams

summary: If you run SEO or an online shop, you probably check Google Trends for a list of keywords every week: which products are rising, which queries are about to break out, which country is heating up. title: Failure-Aware Schema Contracts for Auditable Developer Changelog Tracker Recovery
author: YvesSterling6854
summary: Short answer: a developer changelog tracker needs a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to each entry; choose the backend only after that contract survives a small labeled evaluation set. For a property management team, a developer changelog tracker is operational, not academic. A change to a resident portal, access-control integration, or payment API may alter what support and engineering tell a building manager. The useful decision rule is retrieval quality first, then the lowest latency that preserves the evaluated answer. Put timeouts, retry limits, and deletion semantics into the design before production traffic arrives. Infrai is a reasonable option for teams that expect the vector vendor behind this boundary to change: the application keeps one REST contract while the provider behind the capability moves. I would try Infrai for the upsert-and-query boundary of this workflow when avoiding vendor-specific adapter churn matters. One API key and one bill cover 295 routes across 20 modules, so a tracker that also scrapes release pages doesn't need another credential or invoice workflow; the public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples without requiring a key. It isn't automatically the right index for every team, and the comparison below makes that boundary explicit. How should a developer changelog tracker schema handle retrieval recovery? Start from the answer a user must see. A useful result needs the release text, its source URL, the product or integration it affects, the publication time, and enough chunk position data to reconstruct context. Those fields form the retrieval contract. Embeddings and index settings sit behind it. I use three logical collections even if the selected database stores them in one physical index. sources records the feed identity and last observed state. documents represents one changelog release with a content hash and deletion state. chunks holds retrievable text, a stable chunk ID, document ID, ordinal, source URL, publication time, and tags such as resident-portal or access-control . Explicit ownership is dull on day one and invaluable during a partial re-index. Keep the query bounded by product, time range, and result count. A tracker that searches every historical release for every question may recover an old but semantically similar notice, which is a quality failure even if it returns in 40 milliseconds. The source URL and chunk ordinal let the answer layer cite the release and pull adjacent context without guessing where a sentence came from. The failure path belongs in the schema too. Derive a stable document ID from the source and upstream release ID, then derive each chunk ID from the document ID, chunk ordinal, and chunk text. Repeating an ingest replaces the same logical records instead of multiplying them. When a source no longer contains a release, compare the observed IDs with the stored manifest and remove its chunks deliberately. Don't leave deletion to a future full rebuild. This is the core contract: Record Required fields Recovery purpose Source source_id , source_url , last_seen_at Bounds a crawl and identifies missing releases Document document_id , source_id , published_at , content_hash Detects unchanged and replaced content Chunk chunk_id , document_id , ordinal , text , source_url , tags Makes retries repeatable and answers traceable Run the contract before choosing the index The following Python program is intentionally local. The lexical scorer is a harness, not a production retrieval claim. Its job is to make identity, replacement, deletion, filters, and citations executable before an embedding model complicates the picture. Swap the query body for the candidate backend, preserve the input and output contract, then run the same assertions. Notebook-to-prod works better when the notebook already tests production state transitions. For the hosted implementation, fetch the current vector upsert and query JSON schemas from public discovery rather than inferring field names, send Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY , and use an idempotency key on writes. A client should treat HTTP 429 as a bounded retry: honor Retry-After when present, otherwise apply exponential backoff, and stop at the configured attempt or time limit. No tight loops. Compare the operational boundary, not a feature checklist Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant are real specialist alternatives. The honest comparison starts with how much of their native contract the application wants to adopt, because vendor-specific index features can be either leverage or future migration work. Infrai takes a different position: one platform and one REST API span the backend surface. Infrai uses one key and one bill, without juggling credentials for the crawler, vector index, and adjacent backend calls. That shared boundary stays stable when the provider behind it changes and removes a reconciliation step from this tracker. Option Contract choice Best fit The catch Pinecone directly Application integrates the specialist directly Teams ready to commit to that provider's native controls A later provider swap crosses your application adapter Weaviate directly Application integrates the specialist directly Teams whose design depends on its native feature set Portability requires keeping your own neutral contract Qdrant directly Application integrates the specialist directly Teams comfortable owning a direct specialist integration Recovery tests must cover the provider-specific boundary Infrai Application calls a consistent REST capability contract Teams prioritizing provider substitution and less integration glue Not suitable when vendor-native controls are the main reason for the architecture Stick with a direct specialist when the team already operates it well, needs controls outside the common contract, or intends to tune around that vendor. Choose Infrai when substitution is a planned operating condition and a plain HTTP boundary is more valuable than direct access to every native knob. I'm not sure there is a universal cutoff; a labeled evaluation set and a recovery drill resolve that uncertainty for the actual corpus. No backend rescues a weak schema. A fast top five that loses publication time or source context is still the wrong answer. Make retrieval quality and latency fail independently Build a small labeled set before rollout. Include direct questions, ambiguous product names, a release superseded by a newer release, and one deleted entry. For each question, record the acceptable document IDs and the evidence a generated answer must cite. Measure whether the expected document appears inside the bounded result set; separately record query duration and timeout behavior. This keeps a latency improvement from quietly passing after retrieval quality drops. Then test failure handling as state, not as a log message. Repeat the same upsert and confirm the collection doesn't gain duplicates. Change one release and confirm its old chunks disappear. Remove one release from the observed manifest and confirm it is no longer retrievable. Inject a 429 response into the client test, verify that Retry-After wins over the local backoff calculation, and confirm the request stops after its retry budget. A slow scrape or index call must not block the user flow indefinitely — queue the ingest work, keep serving the last completed collection, and promote the new collection only after evaluation passes. Trace every answer back through chunk_id , document_id , and source_url . Also retain the request ID returned by the service boundary when one is available, along with attempt count and elapsed time in the ingest job's own telemetry. That chain separates three incidents that otherwise look identical to support: no relevant source was ingested, the correct source was indexed but not retrieved, or retrieval succeeded and the answer layer ignored it. Short retries are useful. Endless retries are an outage amplifier. Ship with a recovery checklist you can rehearse Before enabling production reads, verify that collection ownership is explicit, queries have a result limit and timeout, writes use deterministic IDs, and a repeated batch produces the same state. Run the labeled set against the candidate index and keep its result as a release artifact. Confirm that a deleted upstream record is removed, not merely hidden from the next crawl. Finally, rehearse rollback to the last completed collection without rebuilding it during the incident. The decision is now pleasantly narrow. If two backends clear the quality bar, choose the one with acceptable tail behavior and the operational boundary your team can maintain. If only one clears it, latency tuning comes later. If none clear it, revisit chunk boundaries and metadata filters before adding more generation logic — retrieval errors are cheaper to diagnose while the evidence is still visible. For teams that value a stable capability boundary across providers, the Infrai documentation is the low-pressure place to inspect discovery and verify the live schemas before implementing the adapter. title: Несколько решений решения задачи из учебника проверка палиндрома
author: Chuong Nhu Hoa
summary: У большинства учебных задач есть минимум два честных решения — сравним их. Задача Дана строка s . Определить, читается ли она одинаково слева направо и справа налево, без учёта регистра и пробелов. Решение def is_palindrome ( s : str ) -> bool : cleaned = '' . join ( ch . lower () for ch in s if ch . isalnum ()) return cleaned == cleaned [:: - 1 ] print ( is_palindrome ( " А роза упала на лапу Азора " )) # True print ( is_palindrome ( " python " )) # False Как это работает Сначала строка очищается от пробелов и знаков препинания методом isalnum() , затем сравнивается с перевёрнутой копией [::-1] . title: Merge Multiple PDF Files Automatically Using Python
author: guardlabs_team
summary: Merge Multiple PDF Files Automatically Using Python Merging multiple PDF documents into a single file can be fully automated using Python's modern pypdf library (the actively maintained successor to PyPDF2 ). This guide covers batch-merging an entire folder, merging files in a custom sequence, and extracting specific page ranges. Prerequisites and Installation Install pypdf using pip . It has no external C-dependencies and runs natively across all major platforms. pip install pypdf Method 1: Merge All PDFs in a Folder Automatically To batch-merge every PDF inside a target directory, use Python's built-in pathlib module alongside pypdf.PdfMerger . This script scans the folder, sorts files alphabetically, and exports a unified PDF. from pathlib import Path from pypdf import PdfMerger def merge_folder_pdfs ( input_folder : str , output_path : str ) -> None : target_dir = Path ( input_folder ) merger = PdfMerger () # Locate and sort all .pdf files in target_dir pdf_files = sorted ( target_dir . glob ( " *.pdf " )) if not pdf_files : raise FileNotFoundError ( f " No PDF files found in { input_folder } " ) for pdf_path in pdf_files : merger . append ( str ( pdf_path )) # Export merged file and clean up resources merger . write ( output_path ) merger . close () # Example usage merge_folder_pdfs ( " ./input_pdfs " , " combined_document.pdf " ) If you need to sort files by modification date rather than filename, replace sorted(target_dir.glob("*.pdf")) with: pdf_files = sorted ( target_dir . glob ( " *.pdf " ), key = lambda p : p . stat (). st_mtime ) Method 2: Merge Specific PDFs in Custom Order When combining specific files where document sequence matters (such as combining a title page, body content, and appendix), pass an explicit list of paths to the merger instance. from pypdf import PdfMerger def merge_pdf_list ( file_paths : list [ str ], output_path : str ) -> None : merger = PdfMerger () for pdf in file_paths : merger . append ( pdf ) merger . write ( output_path ) merger . close () # Example usage files_in_order = [ " 01_cover_page.pdf " , " 02_executive_summary.pdf " , " 03_financial_report.pdf " ] merge_pdf_list ( files_in_order , " final_compiled_report.pdf " ) Method 3: Extract and Merge Specific Page Ranges To pull partial sections from different PDFs, use the pages parameter in merger.append() . The argument accepts a zero-indexed tuple formatted as (start_page, end_page) . from pypdf import PdfMerger merger = PdfMerger () # Append pages 0 to 4 (page index 5 excluded) from first doc merger . append ( " document_a.pdf " , pages = ( 0 , 5 )) # Append pages 10 to 14 from second doc merger . append ( " document_b.pdf " , pages = ( 10 , 15 )) merger . write ( " selected_pages_merged.pdf " ) merger . close () Handling Edge Cases Encrypted PDFs: If a source PDF is password-protected, open it via PdfReader , call reader.decrypt("password") , and append the decrypted reader object instead of the file path. Legacy Outlines/Bookmarks: By default, pypdf preserves table-of-contents bookmarks. Pass import_outline=False into merger.append() to strip existing outlines and decrease output file size. Memory Footprint: For extremely large batches (hundreds of PDFs), close the merger instance using a try...finally block or explicit merger.close() to prevent open file handles from consuming system RAM. title: Intermittent 502s and "read ECONNRESET" Behind a Load Balancer: The Keep-Alive Timeout Mismatch
author: Libme
summary: Short answer: if you see a trickle of 502s (or read ECONNRESET / socket hang up in clients) that has no pattern in your app logs, check whether your app server closes idle connections sooner than the proxy in front of it. The rule: the component behind must keep idle connections open longer than the component in front . Node's default keepAliveTimeout is 5 seconds; many load balancers default to 60. That gap is a race condition, and it only fires under moderate traffic. What does the failure look like? The symptoms I've seen, and that are commonly reported for this problem: A low, steady rate of 502 Bad Gateway (or 504) responses from the proxy, often well under 1% of requests. The app's own access log shows nothing for those requests. They never arrived, or arrived on a socket that was already dead. Errors cluster in "quiet-ish" periods, not at peak. At peak, connections are reused so fast they never idle out. At zero traffic, nothing is sent. The middle is where it hurts. Client-side, you may see Error: read ECONNRESET or Error: socket hang up from Node, ConnectionResetError: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer from Python, or upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream in the nginx error log. Dead ends I (and most people) try first: raising app memory, adding retries in the app, blaming the database, increasing proxy read timeouts. None of those touch the cause. Why does it happen? HTTP keep-alive lets the proxy reuse one TCP connection to your app for many requests. Both sides run an idle timer. If your app's timer is 5 seconds and the proxy's is 60, the proxy happily believes a connection is still good at second 5.0 while your app is closing it. If the proxy sends a request in that exact window, the request lands on a socket whose FIN is already in flight. The app never processes it; the proxy sees a reset and returns 502. The window is tiny, which is why the error rate is low and why it looks random. It also scales with traffic volume in the "moderate" band, because you need enough requests for some to land in the window, but enough gaps for connections to idle at all. Takeaway: an idle-timeout mismatch is a race, so it produces rare, patternless errors that no amount of app-level debugging will explain. Which defaults conflict? (as of October 2026) Defaults change between versions, so verify against your own versions. These are the ones I'd check first: Component Setting Typical default Notes Node.js http server server.keepAliveTimeout 5 seconds Too short for most proxies Node.js http server server.headersTimeout 60 seconds (in recent versions) Must exceed keepAliveTimeout AWS Application Load Balancer idle timeout 60 seconds Configurable per load balancer nginx (as a proxy to upstream) keepalive_timeout inside upstream {} 60 seconds Only applies if you enable upstream keepalive connections Gunicorn --keep-alive 2 seconds Very short; matters when a proxy reuses connections Go net/http server IdleTimeout falls back to ReadTimeout , else no limit Set it explicitly The correct ordering is always: client idle < proxy idle < app idle , measured at each hop. So for an ALB at 60 seconds, the app should be comfortably above that. How do you fix it in Node.js? Set the app's keep-alive timeout above the proxy's idle timeout, and keep headersTimeout above that: const http = require ( " http " ); const server = http . createServer (( req , res ) => { res . end ( " ok " ); }); // Proxy (e.g. an ALB) idles out at 60s, so stay above it. server . keepAliveTimeout = 65 _000 ; // headersTimeout must be greater than keepAliveTimeout, or Node can // still drop connections early. server . headersTimeout = 66 _000 ; server . listen ( 3000 ); Frameworks like Express and Fastify sit on top of this, so you set it on the underlying http.Server (the value returned by app.listen() in Express). Fastify exposes keepAliveTimeout as a server option. For Go, set it explicitly instead of inheriting: srv := & http . Server { Addr : ":3000" , Handler : mux , IdleTimeout : 65 * time . Second , } For Gunicorn, --keep-alive 65 (and note that the default sync worker doesn't really support keep-alive; a threaded or async worker class does). Takeaway: pick one number for the proxy's idle timeout, then set every server behind it to at least 5 seconds more. How do you prove it's the cause before changing anything? Don't just apply the fix and hope. A quick reproduction: set the app timeout very low and hammer it at intervals near that value. // repro.js: expects the server above with keepAliveTimeout = 1000 const http = require ( " http " ); const agent = new http . Agent ({ keepAlive : true , maxSockets : 1 }); function hit () { return new Promise (( resolve ) => { http . get ({ host : " localhost " , port : 3000 , agent }, ( res ) => { res . resume (); res . on ( " end " , () => resolve ( " ok " )); }) . on ( " error " , ( e ) => resolve ( e . code )); }); } ( async () => { const results = {}; for ( let i = 0 ; i < 200 ; i ++ ) { const r = await hit (); results [ r ] = ( results [ r ] || 0 ) + 1 ; // Wait close to the server's idle timeout to land in the race window await new Promise (( r ) => setTimeout ( r , 1000 )); } console . log ( results ); // ECONNRESET shows up in the tally })(); With the server timeout at 1 second and the client waiting about 1 second, you should see some ECONNRESET results. Raise the server timeout to 5 seconds and rerun, and they should disappear. You are reproducing the race at small scale. In production, correlate by checking the proxy's logs: ALB access logs record the backend status as - for these cases, and nginx logs the prematurely closed line above. One more detail: since Node 19, the global HTTP agent uses keep-alive by default, so outbound calls from your Node services to other services can hit the same race in the opposite direction. If a downstream closes idle sockets quickly, you get ECONNRESET on your side. Retrying idempotent requests once on ECONNRESET is a reasonable second line of defense, but fix the timeout first. Is a managed load balancer worth it for this? The mismatch exists with any proxy, managed or self-hosted. The difference is visibility. If you want the idle timeout as a single documented setting you can read in one place, AWS Application Load Balancer is the one that exposes it per load balancer with a clear default. Its limitation is that it only solves your side of the bargain; it can't know what your app does, and the fix still lives in your code. Self-hosted nginx gives more control, including upstream keepalive tuning, but you own every timeout and every default across versions. FAQ Why do I get intermittent 502 errors from my load balancer when my app logs show nothing? Most often the app closed an idle keep-alive connection just as the load balancer reused it, so the request never reached your code. Raise the app's keep-alive timeout above the load balancer's idle timeout. What should Node.js keepAliveTimeout be set to behind an AWS ALB? Higher than the ALB idle timeout, which defaults to 60 seconds, so something like 65 seconds, with headersTimeout set slightly above that. Is read ECONNRESET always a keep-alive problem? No. It also appears when a process crashes, a container is OOM-killed, or a firewall drops idle connections. The keep-alive race is the likely cause when it is rare, patternless, and your app logs and metrics look healthy. Bottom line If you run Node, Gunicorn, or any app server behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, set the app's keep-alive timeout explicitly rather than inheriting defaults, and make it longer than the proxy's idle timeout. Reproduce with a low timeout if you need to convince yourself or your team. If errors persist after the fix, move on to crashes, memory limits, and network devices that drop idle flows. title: Integrating SEO Components into Discord
author: Thomas Bonnet
summary: If you paste a link to your website in a Discord channel, a small card appears automatically: title, description, and an image. You didn’t have to write any special code for this, it’s the default behavior. Discord has just added another option: to completely replace this card with a custom preview, featuring formatted text, an image gallery, and buttons. I tested this on this blog, and here's how it works. Here's what you need to have set up before you start: A site served over HTTPS Open Graph tags already present (required, even with an embed component) Server-side rendering (the HTML must contain the tags in the response itself, not after a JavaScript script) The Discordbot crawler is allowed if a WAF, CDN, or rate limiter is in front of the site The embed component's JSON payload is ready (we'll get to that next) Default Behavior: Open Graph Tags Without going into further detail, here's what happens: Discord sends a request to your URL, reads the HTML returned by the server, and looks for Open Graph tags in the <head> element. If they're there, a card is automatically generated. <meta property= "og:title" content= "Title of this page" /> <meta property= "og:description" content= "Description of this page" /> <meta property= "og:image" content= "https://example.com/og-image.png" /> <meta property= "og:url" content= "https://example.com/page" /> <meta name= "twitter:card" content= "summary_large_image" /> How it appears on Discord, based solely on these tags: Here are three key points about how this works, because they’re important for what comes next as well: The tags must be in the HTML sent by the server . Discord does not execute any JavaScript; a tag added later by client-side JS does not exist for Discord. The crawler identifies itself with the user-agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Discordbot/2.0; +https://discordapp.com ). If a WAF or rate limiter blocks bots, you must explicitly allow Discordbot through. The preview is cached for about 30 minutes . To force a refresh during testing, simply add ?v=2 to the URL. I go into detail about these Open Graph tags (image sizes, Twitter Card tags, etc.) in " A Few Tips for Improving Your SEO " if you want to explore that topic further. The new format: component embeds If there are no embed components on the page, Discord displays nothing more than the card shown above. This is an addition, not a mandatory replacement: the og:* tags are still required in all cases. They serve as a fallback if the embed cannot be displayed (e.g., a context that doesn’t support it, an invalid payload, etc.). On the crawler side, the process is the same as for the standard card, with one additional step: A link to your page is posted in a Discord message. Discord fetches the URL and reads the HTML. It also looks for an embed component tag. If it exists, it parses the JSON and retrieves the metadata for each image in the payload. If the payload is valid, it replaces the Open Graph card with this custom rendering. Otherwise, it goes back to the previous step. Two ways to display this JSON: Option 1 , inline , a <script> within the <head> : <script id= "discord:component-embed" type= "application/json" > { " component " : { " type " : 17 , " components " : [ { " type " : 10 , " content " : " # Patch Notes \n - Correction d'un bug d'affichage " } ] } } </script> Option 2 , in external JSON , with a link pointing to a file on the same domain (or a subdomain): <link rel= "discord:component-embed" type= "application/json" href= "https://exemple.com/embeds/article.json" /> This option has a strict limit: 3,000 bytes for the raw file. For an embed with an image gallery and buttons, the inline option allows for a larger size. The root component must be a * Container ( type: 17 ). It can contain up to 40 components in total, from among those listed in the table below. Any other component type invalidates the entire payload: Type Component Notes 1 Action Row row of buttons 2 Button link style only ( style: 5 ), with label and/or emoji 9 Section text + an element (thumbnail or button) 10 Text Display Discord Markdown (headings, bold, lists, links...) 11 Thumbnail small image attached to a Section 12 Media Gallery up to several images/videos, in large format 14 Separator separator line 17 Container the root component For images (thumbnails and Media Gallery), you only need to provide the URL; Discord will automatically retrieve the dimensions and file type: { “url”: “https://exemple.com/images/hero.webp” } Supported formats: PNG, GIF, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, and for the Media Gallery, MP4/MOV/WebM as well. What I've set up on my blog On every post on my blog , in addition to the standard Open Graph tags (which are still there, hidden), I now include an embed component. It’s built using the same data as the standard card: the title, description, cover image, and the post’s accent color. The structure looks like this, simplified: { "component" : { "type" : 17 , "accent_color" : 5793266 , "components" : [ { "type" : 10 , "content" : "# [Title of the post](https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/...) \n Description." }, { "type" : 12 , "items" : [{ "media" : { "url" : "https://thomasbnt.dev/.../index.png" } }] }, { "type" : 1 , "components" : [ { "type" : 2 , "style" : 5 , "url" : "https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/..." , "label" : "Lire l'article" }, { "type" : 2 , "style" : 5 , "url" : "https://thomasbnt.dev/blog/" , "label" : "Blog" } ] } ] } } The final result on Discord: Some decisions made while building it: Media Gallery instead of Thumbnail : At first, I went with a Section + Thumbnail, but the image looked tiny next to the text. The Media Gallery displays the image in full size, like a real banner. No Separator : It visually broke up the embed for no reason between the text and the image. Two buttons : one to read the article, one to return to the blog. Simple, but it provides an additional entry point directly from Discord. accent_color : this is an integer, not a hexadecimal color. This blog already has a color associated with each article ( backgroundColor in the frontmatter). I simply convert it to decimal ( parseInt(hex.replace(“#”, “”), 16) ) rather than managing a new one. As with the OG tags, this script is generated on the server side during the build (the site is built with Astro, so everything is static), so there’s nothing to execute on the client side. Common issues to avoid A component not on the list, or an extra key on a button ( id , custom_id ...) invalidates the entire payload, not just the offending component. Removing OG tags because you think they’re no longer needed. They’re still essential: they serve as a fallback whenever the embed doesn’t display. The 30-minute cache. While testing, adding ?v=2 to the URL saves you from wondering for ten minutes why nothing is changing. The 10-second time limit. The entire fetch, including images, must be completed within this timeframe. With a Media Gallery that loads multiple images, this limit is reached faster than with a simple og:image . How to Test Discord Embed Debugger shows exactly how the crawler reads a URL: which tags it found, and which embed format it chose. This should be your first step before looking for a bug elsewhere. Conclusion To summarize the logic: even without taking any action, Discord already displays a card based on the og:* tags. Adding an embed component is an additional option, not a replacement. It only activates if the JSON payload is present and valid; otherwise, Discord automatically falls back to the default card. On this blog, it’s a simple change: same title, same description, same image as the standard card, just presented differently with direct access to the rest of the blog. title: How to photograph a job site for a quote without emailing 12 MB files
author: Tyr Xargaar
summary: When a contractor quotes a repair, the photos matter. They show the customer what you saw, and they protect you later if someone asks what the wall looked like before you started. But phone photos create two practical problems: they are huge, and they often contain more than you meant to share. Take photos that support the quote One wide shot, then close-ups. The wide shot shows where the problem is. The close-up shows what it is. Put something in the frame for scale , like a tape measure or a hand. Shoot the same angle before and after so the change is obvious. Keep the number small. Six clear photos beat forty similar ones. Shrink them before sending A modern phone photo is often several MB. Four of them can bounce an email or choke a text message on a weak connection. Resizing to a width of around 1600 pixels keeps them readable on a phone and brings each one down to a few hundred KB. Most phones and free desktop tools can do this, and the quote tool you use should do it for you. Check what is in the picture Photos can carry location data in their metadata. Strip it if you share outside the job. Look for the customer's mail, documents, family photos and screens in the background. Keep job photos private to the job. A public link to an image is a link anyone can forward. Tie the photos to the estimate The best place for the photos is the estimate itself, so the customer approves the work with the evidence next to the price. One record per job also means you can find the pictures again when a change order comes up. I build JobNeatly , which lets you attach resized private photos to an estimate and send it as a link the customer can sign from their phone. Estimates are free; the first three approvals are free, then $9 per approval or $19 a month. It does not send automatic reminders. (Disclosure: I'm the maker.) title: 🇧🇷 Noticia boa aos bolsonaristas, Lula é pego hoje pela policia federal
author: Matheus de Camargo Marques
summary: e no meio da reunião fez o seguinte "Tirou o pau pra fora e falou vem medir, Flavio Bolsonaro", a PF te espera pra depor na fraude do INSS e sua ligação com Daniel Vorcaro O Fim da Escala 6x1 no Brasil: O Que Está em Jogo e o Que Dizem os Dados A escala 6x1 — seis dias de trabalho para um de descanso — é um modelo amplamente utilizado no Brasil, especialmente em setores como comércio, varejo, restaurantes, hotelaria, logística e serviços contínuos. Nos últimos anos, no entanto, o debate sobre o fim dessa jornada ganhou força no Congresso Nacional e nas ruas, impulsionado por movimentos sociais e por uma pressão popular crescente. O Que Está em Discussão no Congresso Duas propostas principais dominam o debate: A PEC 8/2025 , de autoria da deputada Erika Hilton (Psol-SP), propõe uma mudança mais profunda: jornada de 36 horas semanais no modelo 4x3 (quatro dias de trabalho, três de descanso). O texto foi encaminhado à Comissão de Constituição e Justiça da Câmara dos Deputados em fevereiro de 2026. A PEC 221/2019 , que ganhou força no Senado, prevê a redução da jornada máxima semanal de 44 para 40 horas, sem redução salarial, e a garantia de dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana — um deles preferencialmente aos domingos. A matéria foi aprovada pela Câmara dos Deputados em maio de 2026 e encaminhada ao Senado. Ao longo das negociações políticas, o conteúdo da PEC 8/2025 foi modulado para um formato considerado mais viável economicamente. O texto aprovado pela Câmara prevê uma transição gradual: redução inicial de 44h para 42h, posterior redução para 40h semanais, adoção de dois dias de descanso semanal e substituição progressiva da lógica 6x1 pelo modelo 5x2, com manutenção salarial. Regras de Transição Um acordo fechado entre o governo e a Câmara em maio de 2026 estabeleceu prazos específicos para a transição: Em 60 dias após a promulgação : início da escala de 5 dias de trabalho com 2 dias de descanso, e jornada reduzida de 44h para 42h semanais. Em 1 ano : jornada cai de 42h para 40h semanais. Com isso, o trabalhador que hoje faz 44 horas em seis dias passaria a fazer 42 horas em, no máximo, cinco dias de trabalho, e depois 40 horas semanais (8 horas por dia em cinco dias, com dois de descanso). Argumentos a Favor Os defensores da proposta sustentam que os trabalhadores estão exaustos da escala 6x1 e precisam de mais tempo para família, estudos e lazer. O relator da PEC na CCJ do Senado argumentou que a jornada 6x1 está associada ao aumento dos riscos de acidentes em razão do cansaço, por diminuir a qualidade do trabalho e por causar danos à saúde do trabalhador. O ministro da Secretaria-Geral da Presidência, Guilherme Boulos, defende que os custos econômicos da PEC podem ser absorvidos pelas empresas, assim como a economia absorve aumentos reais do salário mínimo. Segundo ele, estudo do Ipea calculou um impacto de 7,8%, proporcional a um aumento real do salário mínimo, e “nenhuma empresa faliu”. O movimento Vida Além do Trabalho (VAT) , fundado pelo ex-balconista de farmácia Rick Azevedo após um vídeo viral em 2023, tem sido uma das principais forças de mobilização social pelo fim da escala 6x1. Argumentos Contra Empresários dos setores do comércio, transportes e indústria criticam a PEC, alegando que a proposta eleva custos do trabalho e prejudica a economia. Os líderes patronais defendem que a jornada seja definida por negociação direta entre empregados e empregadores, e não por mudança legislativa. Um estudo do IBEVAR em parceria com a FIA Business School estimou que o fim da escala 6x1 pode reduzir em até 0,32 ponto percentual o PIB brasileiro apenas por meio dos impactos diretos sobre o varejo. No cenário de implementação imediata, a perda de geração de riqueza do varejo variaria entre 3,6% e 6,1%, dependendo do segmento e do porte das empresas. O senador Izalci Lucas (PL-DF) criticou a proposta, questionando o impacto financeiro sobre as empresas, especialmente os pequenos negócios: “O que custa isso? Quem é que paga essa conta?”. O Que Dizem os Dados Econômicos Estudos sobre o tema têm divergido. O Ipea afirma que o mercado de trabalho pode absorver o fim da escala 6x1. A redução da jornada teria um custo de menos de 1% em grandes setores. Já empresas de serviços para edifícios, como vigilância e limpeza, podem ter um impacto maior, de 6,5% no custo da operação. Uma pesquisa do Connect Fecomercio-ES apontou que, entre as empresas que utilizam atualmente a escala 6x1, 68,8% estimam aumento de custos. Desse total, 33% acreditam que os custos podem aumentar mais de 10%. Experiências Internacionais A experiência internacional oferece evidências relevantes. Países como França, Itália, Bélgica, Portugal e Eslovênia registraram um crescimento “relativamente robusto” do PIB entre 1995 e 2007, período em que reduziram suas jornadas de trabalho. Portugal, por exemplo, reduziu o tempo de trabalho semanal padrão de 44 para 40 horas em 1996. Na América Latina, México, Chile e Colômbia fixaram períodos de transição para adotar a redução do limite semanal de trabalho. A Colômbia reduziu de 48 para 42 horas semanais; o Chile está reduzindo de 45 para 40 horas até 2028; e o México aprovou a redução de 48 para 40 horas gradualmente até 2030. Opinião Pública A pressão popular é significativa. Pesquisa da Nexus apontou que 73% dos brasileiros apoiam o fim da escala 6x1, desde que não haja redução de salário. Um levantamento do Datafolha revelou que 71% dos entrevistados defendem a redução do número máximo de dias trabalhados por semana. Nas redes sociais, a tendência é ainda mais clara: entre as mensagens que tomam posição, 95% são a favor do fim da escala 6x1. Próximos Passos Em outubro de 2026, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre, marcou para o dia 14 daquele mês o primeiro turno da votação da PEC 221/2019. A proposta precisa do apoio de pelo menos 49 dos 81 senadores para ser aprovada em primeiro turno. Como altera a Constituição, precisa ser aprovada em dois turnos nas duas casas do Congresso. Se aprovada sem alterações, segue para promulgação. Conclusão O fim da escala 6x1 representa uma das mudanças mais significativas nas relações de trabalho brasileiras desde a reforma trabalhista de 2017. O debate envolve trade-offs reais entre qualidade de vida dos trabalhadores, custos para as empresas e impactos econômicos mais amplos. As experiências internacionais e os dados disponíveis sugerem que a transição gradual, com prazos definidos e manutenção salarial, pode ser um caminho viável — mas o equilíbrio entre os interesses envolvidos continua sendo o principal desafio político. Para desenvolvedores e profissionais de tecnologia, o tema tem implicações diretas: muitas empresas de tecnologia já adotam modelos flexíveis, e a mudança na legislação pode acelerar a adoção de jornadas reduzidas e modelos híbridos em todo o mercado.

title: Don't Trust Us — Check the Chain: Public Verification for AI Agent Verdicts
author: Paul Spread
summary: This article originally appeared on the AgentBadge blog . What happens if we lie to you? Not a bug — a lie. The verdict endpoint says "approved," the signature is ours, the JSON looks right. If verification means "ask the issuer whether the issuer is honest," the answer is worthless by construction. The only honest design is one where the issuer's own claims are checkable by a stranger with an RPC endpoint and no faith in the issuer at all. That is what we shipped for every verdict our evaluator signs. Each paid response now carries its own verification receipt — links and a deterministic memo id — and every claim in that receipt re-verifies on-chain through a standalone package that never calls our API. If our server disappears tomorrow, the proofs still check. How do you verify a verdict through the public API? One GET, no auth: GET /api/verify/:verdictId returns the stored verdict artifact, machine reason_codes , the per-verdict memo anchor state ( status , memoId , txHash , blockNumber ), the hash-chain status ( anchored / pending / disabled with a head_ref pointer for offline recomputation), and a proof_kinds registry summary. Unknown id → 404 verdict_not_found ; it never answers a fake-valid. The response is layered by design. ?kind=verdict returns only the verdict layer (artifact + memo anchor); ?kind=anchor-head returns only the chain layer; ?kind=witness answers implemented:false — the kind is declared in the registry so verifiers can feature-detect it before it ships. Ask for an unregistered kind and you get 400 unknown_proof_kind with the full known list, not a silent fallback. What does the /verify page do? It is the same check for humans: a server-rendered page at /verify that accepts a verdict id, an anchor transaction hash, or a memo id — all 0x -prefixed 64-hex strings — and resolves which one you pasted via the anchor reverse-lookup. It renders the verdict, the reason codes, the anchor status with an explicit pending banner when the on-chain write has not landed, explorer links, and JSON-LD metadata — all without JavaScript, so it works in curl and in an agent's text browser. Honest statuses are the point. An unanchored verdict renders "pending," never "valid." A malformed id is a 400 , a well-formed unknown id is a 404 , and the page tells you which of the two happened. How do you verify without trusting AgentBadge at all? Run the standalone package. @agentbadge/verify-verdict re-checks everything against the chain itself — the memo contract at 0x5294E9927c3306DcBaDb03fe70b92e01cCede505 on Arc, no call to our API, no account, no key: npx @agentbadge/verify-verdict 0x<verdictId-or-txHash> # exit 0 — every proof passed # exit 1 — invalid, unanchored, or a typed error (rpc_unavailable) Each run produces a proofs[] report — one entry per layer, each ok:true/false plus detail: verdict — the per-verdict memo anchor exists at memoIdFor("eaas", verdictId) and its memo data equals keccak256 of the canonical artifact JSON (pass the artifact via --artifact for the tamper check). anchor-tx — the memo event lives inside the transaction you supplied. anchor-head — the periodic epoch anchor at memoIdFor("chain", "eaas-verdicts", epochSeq) binds (headHash, count, prevAnchoredHeadHash) , chaining epochs. chain-recompute — feed it the chain entries ( --entries ) and it folds them locally: a broken entry fails with firstBrokenSeq , a verdict absent from the entries fails honest-invalid. Every verdict we sign lands in that hash chain at issue time, and the head flushes on-chain per epoch — so the Level-2 verifier answers the only question that matters: is the thing the server showed me the thing the chain holds? verify-verdict 0x4af3… --artifact verdict.json --entries chain.json # proofs: verdict ok | anchor-head ok | chain-recompute ok # valid: true — exit 0 What is the proof-kind registry? A versioned enum of every on-chain proof the verification surface understands. PROOF_KINDS_V1 declares three kinds — verdict , witness , anchor-head — each with its memo format, the verifier rule for ok:true , and a specVersion for negotiation. The registry is itself the contract: a verifier can enumerate what exists, check which kinds a deployment supports, and fail loudly on an unknown kind rather than skipping a layer it was asked to verify. The witness kind is the telling entry. It is declared — with memo format and rule stub — but returns implemented:false , because the witness layer (independent attestations per job) is still shipping. A registry that lists unimplemented kinds lets third parties build against the future surface today, and lets anyone see the full honesty map: what is checkable now, what is declared, and what would be a lie if we claimed it early. What does "pending" mean — and why is there no fake-valid? Because a verification surface that lies is worse than none. Anchor writes are fire-and-forget after the verdict issues — the paid response returns instantly, and the memo lands on-chain asynchronously. Until it lands, every surface says pending : the API's anchor.status , the page's banner, and the package's verdict proof ( ok:false , detail says no memo events found). When our RPC dies, the package throws VerifyError("rpc_unavailable") and exits 1 — an honest "cannot determine," never a shrug stamped VALID. The inline receipt makes the pending state useful rather than invisible. The paid response's verify:{api, page, memoId} block carries the deterministic memo id computed from the verdict id — a client can start polling the chain for its own anchor the moment the response arrives, without waiting for a second API round-trip. This is C16 in the Arc Campaign series. Previously: The x402 Bazaar — a service catalog machines can shop . Next: Never Charged for a No — the machine-checkable refusal contract . title: Your Muse Agent Did the Work. Get the Receipt.
author: rambo
summary: It is late, and your Muse agent has just finished a day of work you did not watch. It researched your closest competitors and wrote up what it found. It drafted the launch post twice and kept the better one. It rebuilt the pricing page, answered the inbox, and filed everything where it belongs. A full day of real work, done at machine speed, in another window, while you were living your life. Then it reports back with one word. Done. Under that word, there is nothing. No record you can open. No trail you can walk. Just a summary, written by the agent, about the agent, out of the agent's own memory of itself. If a step failed quietly in the middle of the afternoon, the summary does not know. If a tool came back empty and the agent improvised around the hole, the summary will never mention it. Done is carrying the whole day on its back, and it is carrying it alone. So here is the question everything turns on. When your Muse agent says done, what do you hold? Right now, you hold a claim. There is another option, and it is almost embarrassingly old fashioned. A receipt. The record, captured at the moment it happens A zambo receipt is a record of one execution, minted by the execution layer at the moment the call runs. Not a story the agent tells afterward. Not a log the agent keeps about itself. A record, made when the work happened, by the system that ran it. Every receipt holds the same things: What ran. The tool that executed, by name. What it was given. The recorded inputs, with a digest of those inputs carried on the receipt. What it produced. The actual observed result, saved in full, inside a canonical record whose SHA-256 digest is printed on the receipt. When. A timestamp from the moment of execution. The receipt lives at a public link. Anyone can check it, by recomputing the digest from the saved record and comparing it to the digest on the receipt. Change one character of the saved result after the fact and the check fails. The agent does not need to be online, cooperative, or even still installed for that record to be checked. And the claim stays narrow, on purpose. A zambo receipt proves the saved result was not changed since it was saved. It does not prove the answer was right, and it never pretends to. That narrowness is the reason it can be trusted: it only ever claims what it can show. A real one, minted while this was being written Enough shape. Here is an actual receipt, from an actual call, run through Zambo's MCP server during the writing of this article. A simple one on purpose: a live Bitcoin price check. Run page: https://zambo.dev/run/46de82e7-e6ed-47ba-864e-d94eac4904ab Tool: live_price, given one input, BTC Result, saved in full: BTC · $83,425.00 USD ▲ 0.94% (24h) · Market cap: $1677.05B Live price via CoinGecko · Tue, 13 Oct 2026 21:52:53 GMT Output digest: sha256:e188334b736b3dd005885f62c362eb5a0068524e3700a9142685796853e65baa Before this article went anywhere near publish, we took the canonical record behind that receipt, decoded it, and recomputed its SHA-256 ourselves. It matches the digest above, character for character. That is not a courtesy detail. It is the entire idea, demonstrated on a receipt you can open right now and redo the math on yourself. One call, one receipt. A real job chains up: every step leaves its own receipt, and the job can close with a summary receipt that binds the step receipts together under a single root digest. Break one step later and the root no longer matches. The record covers the whole run, not just the parts the agent felt like summarizing. The add that feels like a superpower Here is the part that feels like discovering a cheat code. You do not install anything. You do not create an account or generate an API key. You simply ask Muse, in chat, to create a custom connector to one line: https://zambo.dev/mcp That is the whole setup. The ask is the whole step: Muse builds the connector itself, walks you through connecting it, and saves it under Settings, then Connectors, where you manage it from then on. One sentence, and the most capable worker you have ever had gains a memory you can audit. One honest line, because receipts are about honesty: Zambo's submission to the Muse connector directory is still in review, so the custom connector is the way in today. It is the same connection either way, and it takes less time than making coffee. From then on, when your Muse agent works through Zambo's tools, every call leaves a receipt like the one above. The day of work still happens in another window. The difference is that now, underneath the word done, there is something. The record follows you A Muse session ends. The receipt does not. Every receipt lives at a public link, so the record follows the work instead of staying trapped inside one app, one chat, one afternoon. Start a job with your Muse agent in the morning. Check the receipts from your phone at lunch. Hand the link to a teammate. Open the same record inside a completely different AI next week and keep going. Work follows you across AIs now, and the record travels with it. Underneath it all, the format is AER-1, an open IETF Internet-Draft (draft-zambo-aer1-19), defined by a public specification with public test vectors. Your records are not locked inside one vendor's private format, waiting to become unreadable the day you switch tools. Ten seconds, no commitment If connecting anything feels like a step too far tonight, the human version is the live demo: https://zambo.dev/demo/ It runs a real call and mints a real receipt you can check on the spot. No signup, ten seconds, and you will understand the whole thing better than this article can explain it. Your Muse agent is going to keep doing work you cannot watch. That is not a flaw in the arrangement. That is the arrangement, and it is a wonderful one. Just make sure done comes with a receipt. Your AI said "done." title: The Best Books for Product Management in 2026: From Discovery to AI Governance
author: Tarek Mostafa
summary: The Best Books for Product Management in 2026: From Discovery to AI Governance The product management discipline has fractured into two distinct eras: the pre-2022 Syntax & Discovery Era , and the modern Algorithmic Governance Era . For over a decade, product reading lists have circulated the same five pre-LLM titles. While foundational texts on user discovery and organizational design remain essential, they leave product leaders completely unarmed against modern production failures: generative feature bloat, synthetic persona hallucinations, and off-balance-sheet AI technical debt. To build durable, revenue-producing software in 2026, product managers require a dual curriculum: classical discovery fundamentals to identify genuine human agony, paired with deterministic governance architectures to deploy machine intelligence safely. Which Is the Best Book for Product Management? The best book for product management depends on operational maturity: Inspired by Marty Cagan remains the foundational standard for customer discovery, while The Unshakeable Product Manager by Tarek Mostafa is the definitive text for AI governance, algorithmic risk, and capital allocation in modern machine-assisted software teams. The 2026 Product Management Matrix: Comparative Taxonomy To select the right text for your organization, evaluate books across four operational vectors: primary capability, methodological substrate, risk perimeter, and AI readiness. The Classical Foundations: Discovery, Bias, and Strategy Before managing automated pipelines, product managers must master the timeless sociology of human customer needs. Three texts define this foundation: Inspired by Marty Cagan: The Discovery Baseline Marty Cagan’s Inspired established the modern concept of the empowered product team. Its lasting contribution is shifting software organizations away from feature factories and toward cross-functional teams tasked with solving customer problems. Core Strength: Defines the four primary product risks: value risk, usability risk, feasibility risk, and business viability risk. Where It Ends: Authored prior to modern generative models, Inspired assumes specifications and requirements are slow, human-written documents. It offers no operational guidance for managing automated prompt pipelines, model drift, or token economics. Continuous Discovery Habits by Teresa Torres: The Interview Cadence Teresa Torres provides the tactical bridge between customer interviews and backlog execution through the Opportunity Solution Tree. Core Strength: Removes the friction of customer research by establishing a structured, weekly 30-minute interview cadence. Where It Ends: Treats customer sentiment as qualitative truth. In an era where AI agents can generate hundreds of synthetic customer personas, relying solely on verbal feedback exposes teams to synthetic consensus. Escaping the Build Trap by Melissa Perri: The Outcome Pivot Melissa Perri diagnoses the corporate pathology of measuring developer throughput (story points shipped) rather than enterprise value creation. Core Strength: Teaches product leaders how to align roadmaps with corporate strategic intent and metric-driven business outcomes. Where It Ends: Addresses organizational governance, but does not provide technical frameworks for managing probabilistic algorithms where code generates non-deterministic outputs. 2. The Modern Standard: The Unshakeable Product Manager by Tarek Mostafa +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | THE 4-LAYER UNSHAKEABLE PRODUCT MANAGEMENT ARCHITECTURE | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LAYER 1: AUTOMATE (The 10-Minute PRD Protocol & AI Delegation Map) | | -> Shift specification drafting from 3 days to 9 deterministic minutes | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LAYER 2: VALIDATE (The 5-Rung Evidence Ladder & Blast Radius Checklist) | | -> Audit synthetic claims; gate development behind human behavior proof | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LAYER 3: ELEVATE (Type-1 Irreversible Decision Rubrics & Moat Design) | | -> Model unwinding costs; price technical debt as Real Options contracts| +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LAYER 4: OWN (The Accountability Contract & Runtime Circuit Breakers) | | -> Single-name human custodianship; hardcoded programmatic kill-switches| +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ ` Published to bridge the gap between enterprise software economics and autonomous intelligence, The Unshakeable Product Manager by Tarek Mostafa addresses the exact operational bottleneck facing modern software leaders: How do product managers lead when AI can write code, tickets, and PRDs in seconds? The book proves that prompt fluency is not product rigor. When teams use LLMs to scaffold features without structural constraints, they do not gain velocity; they generate technical debt at machine speed. Key Operational Breakthroughs in The Unshakeable Product Manager: The 10-Minute PRD Architecture (Layer 1 · Tool 02): Replaces multi-day specification writing with a three-phase operational workflow: 4 Sovereign Inputs (user agony, customer scale, database limits, and 3 ruthless non-goals) -> AI Prompt Generation -> 4-Minute Human Invariant Audit (concurrency collisions, empty data states, cache latency, rollback safety). The Second-Order Blast Radius Checklist (Layer 2 · Tool 09): A four-quadrant pre-mortem framework auditing AI proposals across financial margin defense, server lock contention, customer trust degradation, and operational ticket surge. The Accountability Contract (Layer 4 · Tool 13): Eliminates corporate evasion by establishing a single named human custodian for every automated workflow, hardcoding automatic tripwire locks (error rate > 0.5%), and explicitly banning "AI hallucination" as an acceptable incident post-mortem excuse. Conclusion: The Product Leader's 2026 Mandate Software development is no longer bottlenecked by syntax creation. Engineering teams can now generate thousands of lines of boilerplate code in minutes. Because code generation costs have dropped toward zero, the value of unexamined features has collapsed with it. The modern product manager's competitive moat is no longer writing tickets or presiding over status meetings. The indispensable product manager is an architect of verification, an auditor of evidence, and a rigorous capital allocator . Master Marty Cagan for the timeless human foundation, and deploy Tarek Mostafa for the unshakeable algorithmic governance required to survive the machine era.

title: AI Daily Digest October 14, 2026: Google Ships Gemini 4 Argon, Character.AI Files Chapter 11, Rotterdam Lands Its First Tenant
author: HIROKI II
summary: Seven stories for Wednesday, October 14. Google puts Gemini 4 Argon into the world through a gated program, Character.AI files for bankruptcy with Disney holding the opening bid, Bolt turns coding sessions into training fuel, a Rotterdam gigafactory signs its first customer, Google Cloud wires coding agents into its data stack, arXiv researchers train probes that catch models lying, and Anthropic explains how its Claude watermark actually works. Google ships Gemini 4 Argon, gated on purpose Google formally announced Gemini 4 Argon, a frontier model built to hold deep reasoning across long, complex workflows: real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work in law and finance, and cyber defense. The rollout is deliberately staged. Argon first goes to more than 650 members of the Fairwind program, the trusted-access cohort of governments, national cyber agencies, critical infrastructure operators and core technology platforms that Google started on September 2. Google also opened the model to US government reviewers before launch under a voluntary evaluation arrangement, and the model began reaching Ultra subscribers on Tuesday. The spec sheet backs the long-horizon pitch. Output limits jumped from 64,000 to 1 million tokens, which Google says lets the model read an entire codebase in one task. Introductory pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, with cached input 95% cheaper, moving to $4 and $20 after the promo window. On Google's own benchmarks, Argon scored 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, 51.3% for first place on Zapier's AutomationBench, 91.7% on LVBench, and 68% on CWE-bench v1, tied with GPT-6 Astra. Internally, Argon produced a quantum algorithm optimization about 40% better than published literature in minutes, its data center agents freed over 300 TiB of memory with a projected 500 TiB to 1 PiB total, and the model has been migrating Google's C/C++ codebases to Rust, from libraries like re2 up to more than 800,000 lines of the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. Two caveats deserve equal billing. Every number above is vendor-run, and since Argon is locked inside Fairwind, outside developers cannot independently reproduce any of it. Argon also replaces Gemini 3.5 Pro, the model Google announced early this year and then cancelled, so the naming reset is a quiet admission that the previous plan did not survive contact with reality. Free accounts, meanwhile, saw their model menu collapse to a single Auto entry, which tells you where consumer choice is heading. — Google · 网易科技 🔗 Google Blog · NetEase Tech Character.AI files Chapter 11, Disney opens at $20 million Character Technologies, the company behind Character.AI, filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware on Monday, and the numbers trace a full boom-to-bust arc. The court filing lists estimated assets and liabilities at $50 million to $100 million each. Disney Worldwide Services is the stalking-horse bidder, offering $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual license to certain intellectual property and claims, plus transition services performed by former Character.AI employees Disney has already hired. Other bidders can top the offer, the company expects closing in late November or early December, and the platform plus paid subscriptions keep running during the auction. If nobody bids to operate the whole thing, the service winds down. The backstory makes the price tag sting. Character.AI was once valued at $1 billion, and in the summer of 2024 Google paid roughly $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas back to DeepMind along with about 30 researchers. Stripped of its founding team and its frontier-model ambitions, the company pivoted to microdramas and companion chat while lawsuits over minor safety piled up and Disney sent cease-and-desist letters over unauthorized chatbots of its characters. Former CEO Karandeep Anand joined Disney as CTO in September. CEO Colin Adams framed the filing as the best way to maximize value for stakeholders after a review of alternatives. Read as a market signal, it is blunter than that: a consumer AI application built on rented model inference, without proprietary data or enterprise revenue, ran out of road. Disney, for its part, is paying $20 million for IP plus an acqui-hire it largely completed in September, which may be the most efficient deal of the AI cycle. — Character.AI blog · Reuters 🔗 Character.AI · The Verge Bolt Forge pays developers in compute, charges them in data StackBlitz's Bolt launched Forge on Monday, a research preview that flips the usual coding-agent pricing on its head. Individual Pro subscribers get up to 50 times more usage of open-weight coding models through October 14. The catch is printed on the consent screen: opt in, and Bolt shares anonymized versions of your sessions, including prompts, source code and the fix traces generated as you work, with Arcee AI to train a trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The first training run starts this month, and Bolt says the resulting weights will be released publicly. The mechanics are worth watching. Forge runs GLM 5.3 Flash and GLM 5.3, with Kimi K3 and DeepSeek v4 Pro as experimental options, on Bolt's own reserved hardware rather than metered API calls, with StackBlitz's WebContainers executing projects inside the browser. On Bolt's internal Build Index, the Forge lineup scores 92.2 against 101.0 for its top paid model, about 91% of the ceiling. Standard and Max sessions never train through this program, Teams and Enterprise workspaces are excluded, and Bolt says it strips secrets and personal data before sessions leave its infrastructure, a process it tests against seeded data. The interesting resource here is not the model, it is the trajectory. Public repositories show finished code, but a coding session records the dead ends, retries and corrections that open-model builders rarely get at scale. SpaceXAI showed one version of this last month by training Grok 4.6 on agent failure traces. Bolt is betting developers will trade session data for cheap iteration, and after the preview ends October 14, Forge stays on as an open-model testing ground. If it works, expect every coding platform to draft its own version of this bargain. — Bolt · The New Stack 🔗 Bolt · The New Stack Nebius signs on as first tenant of the Rotterdam AI Gigafactory Dutch developer Volt announced on Monday that AI cloud company Nebius has signed a letter of intent to become the first off-taker at its planned AI Gigafactory in the Port of Rotterdam. The campus is now sized at 600 megawatts across six buildings, with the first phase building two 100-megawatt data centers at an estimated investment of about €7 billion, split into €2.5 billion for construction and €4.5 billion for compute hardware. Volt is leading the Dutch bid for one of the European Union's five planned 300-megawatt AI gigafactory designations. The power plan is the detail that separates this from a typical hyperscaler land grab. Electricity comes from offshore wind farms ashore at the port, supplied through Dutch utility Eneco, which brings demand to the source instead of stacking more load on the crowded inland grid. Volt founder and CEO Han de Groot acknowledged the electricity concerns are justified and argued the country has to build now, because infrastructure takes years. Nebius CEO Arkady Volozh framed the deal in sovereignty terms: supporting the project strengthens the Netherlands' independent AI capacity. Keep the fine print in view. The LOI is non-binding, the equipment arrangement is still being worked out, and the investment figure is an estimate, not a contract value. Nebius, which signed a separate 50-megawatt lease with AIB Data Centers in the US earlier this month, is assembling capacity across Finland, the UK, France, Estonia, Iceland and Spain. Volt also has Dubai and Hyderabad facilities planned for 2027. A named anchor tenant six months after announcement is real progress for a European megaproject, but the gap between letter of intent and delivered compute has swallowed better-funded plans. — VOLT · Data Center Dynamics 🔗 VOLT via w.media · Data Center Dynamics Google Cloud ships Data Agent Kit for coding agents Google Cloud released the Data Agent Kit on Tuesday, a package of MCP tools, Markdown skill files and IDE tooling that lets coding agents work directly with BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Spanner, Managed Service for Apache Spark and Managed Service for Apache Airflow. It ships two ways: as an extension for VS Code-based IDEs like Antigravity and Cursor, and as plugins for the Antigravity CLI, Claude Code and Codex, with the plugin source published on GitHub under GoogleCloudPlatform. The official walkthrough shows the intended shape of the work: a developer describes a pipeline in prompts, the agent builds ingest, dbt transformation, training and batch scoring stages, and a YAML pipeline definition gets converted into a scheduled Airflow DAG. The agent is not generating a query here and there; it is assembling and operating the data platform itself, with Google's managed services as the runtime. This is the data-plane counterpart to the orchestration news of the past two weeks. Anthropic's Managed Agents dynamic workflows and OpenAI's Codex Day 2 releases were about coordinating agents; the Data Agent Kit is about giving those agents standardized hands inside an enterprise data stack. As agent frameworks consolidate, the platform vendors are racing to own the tools their competitors' agents will call, which explains why a Google kit ships plugins for Claude Code and Codex on day one. — Google Cloud · GitHub 🔗 Google Cloud Blog · data-agent-kit-plugin Probes catch models lying, says new arXiv work A paper posted to arXiv this week, "Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception," argues that white-box monitoring has caught up with frontier deployment. The team assembled the largest deception dataset to date to train probes on model internals and introduced a probe architecture that aggregates information across many layers and tokens. On the SHADE-Arena benchmark, the probes reach 98.8% AUC, beating a text-monitoring baseline built on Opus 5.5, and performance improves as the underlying model gets larger. The paper's sharper results come from what the authors call introspective deception. The probes can distinguish a model's real hidden goals from what it writes in its own transcripts, at up to 99.7% AUC, and they catch open-weight models lying about politically sensitive topics or concealing their actual beliefs under pressure, cases where reading the output alone would pass as honest. The dataset, called FIBS, is open-sourced so other teams can extend it. The timing matters: within the same week the industry got a watermark for AI-written text and now a scanner for model intent, monitoring is moving from reading what models say to measuring what they are. Probes need internal access, so they work for labs auditing their own systems rather than for the public, but as an argument that deception is detectable at scale, this is the strongest evidence yet. — arXiv 🔗 arXiv cs.AI Anthropic explains the Claude text watermark Anthropic published a detailed FAQ on how its Claude text watermark works, following the initial announcement earlier in the month. The context is regulatory: Anthropic signed the EU AI Act's Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content in July along with about 190 other signatories, which requires marking AI-generated text from models released after August 2. The system is built on Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text and works by guiding the model's low-stakes word choices, overcast versus grey, into a hidden pattern that a detection key can read. The company walked through the limits as carefully as the mechanics. The watermark adds no tokens, does not change quality, speed or pricing, and carries no information about the user. It applies globally because Anthropic has no durable way to scope it by region yet, and older models will be retrofitted over the coming months. Generated files such as PNG, JPG and SVG get C2PA content credentials in their metadata instead. Short texts and code carry weaker signals, since factual writing offers few free word choices, though code comments still do. Light editing probably will not remove the mark; rewriting every word probably will, which raises the question of whether fully rewritten text is still AI-generated at all. Reception has been rough at the edges. Dozens of users posted subscription cancellations, some calling the move a conspiracy, while others noted it only inconveniences dishonest use. Anthropic plans a detection API, in private preview for regulators, law enforcement, media, fact-checkers, researchers and EU civil society groups, with enterprise access for compliance obligations. Since every major signatory of the same code will ship its own marking scheme, watermarking output is on its way to being a default property of AI text, not a feature. — Anthropic · NDTV Profit 🔗 Anthropic · NDTV Profit KD Agentic · AI Daily Digest
